claims.claim: Popular entertainment (shows, races, games, spectacles) is mostly harmless fun.

stances.summary: The shows are not innocent fun. A Christian who goes from church to the circus or theatre has gone from God's house to the devil's. We have better shows of our own, and the greatest is the Last Judgment.
stances.quote: For how monstrous it is to go from God's church to the devil's— from the sky to the stye, as they say; to raise your hands to God, and then to weary them in the applause of an actor; out of the mouth, from which you uttered Amen over the Holy Thing, to give witness in a gladiator's favour
stances.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, 1885
stances.original: quale est enim de ecclesia dei in diaboli ecclesiam tendere, de caelo, quod aiunt, in caenum? illas manus quas ad deum extuleris postmodum laudando histrionem fatigare? ex ore, quo Amen in Sanctum protuleris, gladiatori testimonium reddere
stances.context: A whole treatise, written about 197-202 for catechumens and the newly baptized, in Tertullian's catholic period (before his Montanist years; he never softened on this). It covers every kind of show: circus races, theatre, athletics and the gladiators. Chapter 1 opens with "the laws of Christian Discipline, which forbid among other sins of the world, the pleasures of the public shows." Chapter 3 answers fellow Christians who said Scripture never forbids the shows ("the faith of some, either too simple or too scrupulous, demands direct authority from Scripture for giving up the shows"). Chapter 29 offers Christian joys instead ("These are the pleasures, these the spectacles that befit Christian men — holy, everlasting, free.") and chapter 30 pictures the Last Judgment as the greatest show, with persecutors and actors in the flames. He says the same briefly in the Apology, chapter 38: "We renounce all your spectacles, as strongly as we renounce the matters originating them". Latin checked at thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.spect.shtml.

stances.summary: Some believers call the shows innocent relaxation and even quote Scripture for them. They are wrong. Even where the shows are not criminal they are empty, and a Christian has the whole of creation and Scripture to look at instead.
stances.quote: These things, even if they were not dedicated to idols, ought not to be approached and gazed upon by faithful Christians; because, even if they were not criminal, they are characterized by a worthlessness which is extreme, and which is little suited to believers.
stances.translation: Robert Ernest Wallis, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5, 1886 (printed as "On the Public Shows" among treatises attributed to Cyprian)
stances.work: On the Public Shows (De spectaculis), transmitted among the works of Cyprian
stances.context: The treatise came down under Cyprian's name, but most scholars now give it to Novatian (the Roman presbyter who became a rigorist rival bishop in 251 and led a schism). Treat the authorship as probable, not certain. It is valuable because it quotes the other side: Christians who treated the shows "as if the pleasure derived from the public exhibitions might be sought after as being innocent, by way of a mental relaxation" (chapter 1), and who argued from Scripture that "Elias is the charioteer of Israel, and David himself danced before the ark" (chapter 2). It condemns races for sheer waste of mind ("How unprofitable a matter is all this", chapter 5), the stage for teaching vice ("He is learning to do, while he is becoming accustomed to see", chapter 6), and offers the sunrise, the stars and the sea as the Christian's show (chapter 9).

stances.summary: The arena trains men to kill and teaches the crowd to enjoy it. The theatre teaches the sins it shows. What you watch, you learn.
stances.quote: Man is slaughtered that man may be gratified, and the skill that is best able to kill is an exercise and an art. Crime is not only committed, but it is taught.
stances.translation: Robert Ernest Wallis, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5, 1886
stances.work: To Donatus (Ad Donatum; numbered Epistle 1 in ANF)
stances.context: Written about 246, soon after his conversion, as a picture of the world he had left. Section 7 is on the gladiators and beast-fights; section 8 turns to the theatre and mime: "Adultery is learned while it is seen". As bishop he also ruled (Epistle 60 in ANF numbering, to Euchratius) that an actor who still trained boys for the stage could not take communion, and offered church support if he gave it up for poverty's sake. Do not confuse this with the treatise On the Public Shows, which is probably Novatian's.

stances.summary: People call the killing in the arena "sport". It is shared homicide. The stage corrupts and the races drive people mad, so a Christian should avoid all the shows.
stances.quote: And yet they call these sports in which human blood is shed. So far has the feeling of humanity departed from the men, that when they destroy the lives of men, they think that they are amusing themselves with sport, being more guilty than all those whose blood-shedding they esteem a pleasure.
stances.translation: William Fletcher, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 7, 1886
stances.context: Written about 303-311. The chapter takes all three kinds in turn: the arena (watching a killing pollutes the conscience "as much as if he should become a spectator and a sharer of a homicide"), the stage, and the circus ("What else does the practice of the Circensian games contain but levity, vanity, and madness?"). His conclusion: "Therefore all spectacles ought to be avoided". In the same chapter he extends "You shall not kill" so far that he rules out soldiering and capital prosecution for a just man.

stances.summary: Exercise and games you play yourself are good: wrestle, play ball, walk, even fish. But the public spectacles are not recreation. They are a school of lust and cruelty, and a city that takes its pastimes that seriously is not wise.
stances.quote: For if people shall say that they betake themselves to the spectacles as a pastime for recreation, I should say that the cities which make a serious business of pastime are not wise; for cruel contests for glory which have been so fatal are not sport.
stances.translation: William Wilson, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2, 1885
stances.context: Written about 190-200. Clement is the clearest example that opposing the shows was not opposing play. In Book 3, chapter 10 he approves exercise for men: "let some strip and engage in wrestling; let some play at the small ball". In chapter 11 he forbids dice ("The game of dice is to be prohibited") and calls "the racecourse and the theatre the seat of plagues". He answers, in his own words, the exact modern defence that the shows are just recreation. Mark him "disagree" on spectacles and dice, but "for" on sport and play.

stances.summary: "It's only acting" is no defence: the theatre has made many adulterers. Even if it did you no harm, you waste your time and help keep the whole trade going. Enjoy gardens, rivers, your wife and children instead.
stances.quote: What then, one may say, if I point to some, who are nothing hurt by their pastime in that place? In the first place, even this is a hurt, to spend one's time without object or fruit, and to become an offense to others.
stances.translation: George Prevost, revised by M.B. Riddle, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 1 vol. 10, 1888
stances.context: Preached at Antioch about 390; he returns to the theatre and the races again and again across his career. Homily 37 answers the defence directly and wishes the stage gone ("Nay, but it is overthrowing lawlessness, if we do away with these spectacles"), but he also offers innocent pleasures: "go to pleasure grounds, to a river flowing by, and to lakes, take notice of gardens, listen to grasshoppers as they sing". Homily 6 on Matthew, section 10, meets the "it is only acting" excuse: "Nay, tell me not, that what is done is acting; for this acting has made many adulterers, and subverted many families." The same homily (section 8) has the famous "For it is not God that grants to play, but the devil," said to a man who wants "to laugh and to play all my days"; he adds in section 9 that he speaks "not to suppress all laughter". As bishop of Constantinople in 399, when his people left church for the races on Good Friday and the theatre the next day, he threatened to bar them from the church: "Let such people be ejected, so that those of us who are healthy may become more healthy" (Against the Games and Theatres, tr. Mark Vermes 2012, placed in the public domain, https://www.tertullian.org/fathers/chrysostom_against_theatres_and_circuses.htm).

stances.summary: I loved the stage when I was young, and I watched my friend Alypius swear he would keep his eyes shut at the gladiators and then get hooked the moment he looked. The shows do not stay on the surface. They get into you.
stances.quote: For, directly he saw that blood, he therewith imbibed a sort of savageness; nor did he turn away, but fixed his eye, drinking in madness unconsciously, and was delighted with the guilty contest, and drunken with the bloody pastime.
stances.translation: J.G. Pilkington, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 1 vol. 1, 1887
stances.original: ut enim vidit illum sanguinem, immanitatem simul ebibit et non se avertit, sed fixit aspectum et hauriebat furias et nesciebat, et delectabatur scelere certaminis et cruenta voluptate inebriabatur.
stances.context: Written about 397-400. The story is about his friend Alypius (later bishop of Thagaste), who "being utterly opposed to and detesting such spectacles" was dragged into the amphitheatre by friends and promised to stay "absent while present". Augustine himself had loved the theatre before his conversion: "Stage-plays also drew me away, full of representations of my miseries and of fuel to my fire" (Confessions 3.2). Later he writes "It is true that the theatres never now carry me away" (10.35), though he admits that even a dog chasing a hare in a field can still distract him. In City of God 1.32-33 he mocks Romans who fled the sack of Rome in 410 and then ran after the actors in the theatres at Carthage. Latin checked at thelatinlibrary.com/augustine/conf6.shtml.

stances.summary: Laugh and enjoy yourself as much as you like, as long as it is innocent. The shows are not innocent. At baptism we renounced the devil and his pomps and shows, so going back to them is going back to him.
stances.quote: If any one thinks the wickedness of the spectacles a trivial matter, let him consider well all that I have said, and he will see that in them is not pleasure but death.
stances.translation: Eva M. Sanford, On the Government of God, Columbia University Press, 1930 (copyright not renewed; public domain in the USA, as stated at tertullian.org)
stances.work: On the Government of God (De gubernatione Dei)
stances.context: A priest of Marseilles writing about 440 as the Western empire collapsed. Not in the candidate pool, but the fiercest Latin voice after Tertullian. He is careful to say he is not against fun: "Let us laugh indeed, let us rejoice unstintedly, and as constantly as you please, if only we do so innocently." He complains that on feast days "the church is emptied and the circus filled", and mocks the survivors of Trier who asked the emperors for circus games after their city was sacked ("Do you, O citizens of Treves, long for circuses when you have been plundered and captured").

stances.summary: The theatre crowd thinks it is happy, but a theatre full of impure sights is a school of vice. Racing fans cannot even stop racing in their dreams. God's creation is the better show.
stances.quote: They do not know that a theatre full of impure sights is, for those who sit there, a common school of vice; that these melodious and meretricious songs insinuate themselves into men's souls, and all who hear them, eager to imitate the notes of harpers and pipers, are filled with filthiness.
stances.translation: Blomfield Jackson, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 2 vol. 8, 1895
stances.context: Preached at Caesarea about 370, as bishop. The lines open a sermon on creation and set the theatre-goers against his own listeners. He also laughs at racing fans: "Some others, who are wild after horses, think they are backing their horses in their dreams". In passing, not a whole argument.

stances.summary: I cannot stand your races and theatres and the party passion they breed. The worst of it is that we in the Church now behave like circus factions.
stances.quote: I cannot bear your horse races and theatres, and this rage for rivalry in expense and party spirit.
stances.translation: Charles Gordon Browne and James Edward Swallow, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 2 vol. 7, 1894
stances.context: His farewell sermon of 381, leaving the see of Constantinople. The blunt line leads into a picture of church factions behaving like the circus parties ("we neigh against each other"). He compares joining them to a grown man leaving his work to join "children at play in the midst of the market place". Brief and partly figurative.

stances.summary: Let Rome keep its noise, its cruel arena, its raving circus crowds and its theatres. I would rather leave the city for a quiet life of prayer in the country.
stances.quote: Let Rome keep to itself its noise and bustle, let the cruel shows of the arena go on, let the crowd rave at the circus, let the playgoers revel in the theatres and — for I must not altogether pass over our Christian friends — let the House of Ladies hold its daily sittings.
stances.translation: W.H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W.G. Martley, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 2 vol. 6, 1893
stances.context: Written in Rome about 385, urging Marcella to retire to the country. Dismissive rather than argued, with a joke at the gossiping Christian ladies in the same breath.

stances.summary: Spending a fortune on circus games, plays and gladiator shows to win popularity is foolish waste. Real generosity feeds and clothes people.
stances.quote: It is wasteful to spend one's own wealth merely for the sake of gaining the favour of the people. This they do who spend their inheritance on the games of the circus, or on theatrical pieces and gladiatorial shows, or even a combat of wild beasts, just to surpass the fame of their forefathers for these things.
stances.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H.T.F. Duckworth, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 2 vol. 10, 1896
stances.work: On the Duties of the Clergy (De officiis)
stances.context: Written about 388-391 and modelled on Cicero's On Duties, which makes a similar complaint about lavish games. His target is the rich sponsor, not the spectator; the next sentence reads "All this that they do is but foolish". A mild, passing voice.

stances.summary: We are not corrupters. We turn women away from their mad love of theatres and dancing and train young men in self-control.
stances.quote: seeing that, on the contrary, we turn away women from a dissolute life, and from being at variance with those with whom they live, from all mad desires after theatres and dancing, and from superstition
stances.translation: Frederick Crombie, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 4, 1885
stances.context: Written about 248 against the pagan critic Celsus. In passing. Elsewhere (5.42) he praises ancient Israel because "they had neither gymnastic contests, nor scenic representations, nor horse-races". Origen's teaching was condemned long after his death (553), but not on this point.

stances.summary: Actors, charioteers, gladiators and their trainers must give up their trade before they can be made Christians.
stances.quote: A charioteer, likewise, who races or frequents races, must desist or be rejected.
stances.translation: Burton Scott Easton, The Apostolic Tradition of Hippolytus, Cambridge University Press, 1934 (on Project Gutenberg as public domain in the USA)
stances.context: A church order usually dated to the early third century. Its attribution to Hippolytus is disputed; many scholars now treat it as a composite text that grew over time. It survives only in later Latin, Coptic, Arabic and Ethiopic versions, from which Easton translated. The same chapter says "If a man is an actor or pantomimist, he must desist or be rejected" and gives the same rule for gladiators, their trainers and beast-hunters. Easton's "frequents races" may reach spectators, but the list is about trades, so cite it as a rule on performers.

stances.summary: The heretics I am refuting are so careless that some even go to the gladiator shows, a bloody sight hated by God and men.
stances.quote: that bloody spectacle hateful both to God and men, in which gladiators either fight with wild beasts, or singly encounter one another.
stances.translation: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1, 1885
stances.context: Written about 180. A passing judgment, but it is also the earliest evidence that some who called themselves Christians did go: Irenaeus says the Valentinian Gnostics were "the first to assemble" at pagan festivals and "some of them do not even keep away" from the gladiators. That report is an opponent's.

stances.summary: The theatre teaches adultery and the arena turns murder into a paid show. I have rejected all of it.
stances.quote: You slaughter animals for the purpose of eating their flesh, and you purchase men to supply a cannibal banquet for the soul, nourishing it by the most impious bloodshedding.
stances.translation: J.E. Ryland, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2, 1885
stances.location: chapter 23 (chapters 22-24 cover theatre, boxers, gladiators and plays)
stances.context: Written about 165-172 by a pupil of Justin Martyr. Tatian later broke with the Church and led the Encratites, an ascetic sect judged heretical; this work is usually dated before or around the break. He writes as an eyewitness ("I have seen men weighed down by bodily exercise").

stances.summary: We are not even allowed to watch the gladiators, because watching a killing makes you share in it. The other shows are closed to us too, because their songs and plots are full of murder and adultery.
stances.quote: we are forbidden so much as to witness shows of gladiators, lest we become partakers and abettors of murders. But neither may we see the other spectacles, lest our eyes and ears be defiled, participating in the utterances there sung.
stances.translation: Marcus Dods, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2, 1885
stances.context: Bishop of Antioch, writing about 180 to a pagan friend. A short, blunt statement of church discipline, used to rebut the rumour that Christians ate human flesh.

stances.summary: To watch a man killed is much the same as killing him, so we have given up the gladiator shows.
stances.quote: But we, deeming that to see a man put to death is much the same as killing him, have abjured such spectacles.
stances.translation: B.P. Pratten, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2, 1885
stances.context: Addressed about 177 to Marcus Aurelius and Commodus. About the killing-shows only. In the same chapter he ties this to the rejection of abortion and infant exposure: a consistent refusal to take any part in killing.

stances.summary: We keep away from your races, your gladiators and your plays. The races make crowds brawl, the arena teaches murder and the stage acts out adultery.
stances.quote: We therefore, who are estimated by our character and our modesty, reasonably abstain from evil pleasures, and from your pomps and exhibitions, the origin of which in connection with sacred things we know, and condemn their mischievous enticements.
stances.translation: Robert Ernest Wallis, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 4, 1885
stances.context: A Latin dialogue from about 200-240; the speaker is the Christian Octavius. The same passage names all three kinds: "For in the chariot games who does not shudder at the madness of the people brawling among themselves? Or at the teaching of murder in the gladiatorial games?" The dialogue opens with the friends happily watching boys skim stones on the beach at Ostia, a small sign that simple play was not the issue.

stances.summary: The gladiator show was an abominable, impious spectacle. The monk Telemachus died trying to stop it and deserves to be counted a martyr.
stances.quote: There, when the abominable spectacle was being exhibited, he went himself into the stadium, and, stepping down into the arena, endeavoured to stop the men who were wielding their weapons against one another.
stances.translation: Blomfield Jackson, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 2 vol. 3, 1892
stances.context: Written about 449-450 about events around 404. The line records the act of the monk Telemachus, whose own words do not survive; the judgment ("abominable", "impious spectacle") is Theodoret's. Theodoret says the emperor Honorius then ended the gladiator shows; historians treat that as a simplification (see misattributions).

stances.summary: God saved this city through the prayers of the saints, not the circus. Yet the shows now draw bigger crowds than the feasts of the martyrs.
stances.quote: One is ashamed to say it, but one must not keep silence: more is spent upon demons than upon the Apostles, and mad spectacles draw greater crowds than blessed martyrdoms.
stances.translation: Charles Lett Feltoe, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers series 2 vol. 12, 1895
stances.work: Sermon 84 (Concerning the Neglect of the Commemoration)
stances.context: Pope 440-461. Preached when few came to the yearly thanksgiving for Rome's deliverance (probably from the Vandal sack of 455; the date is not certain). He goes on: "The games of the circus-goers or the care of the saints?"

stances.summary: A Christian should have nothing to do with the circus, the theatre, the amphitheatre or the games. Going back to them breaks the promise made at baptism.
stances.quote: These spectacles of cruelty and this gazing at vanities were instituted not only by the vices of men but also by the commands of demons. Therefore a Christian ought to have nothing to do with the madness of the circus, the shamelessness of the theatre, the cruelty of the amphitheatre, the savagery of the arena, the luxury of the games.
stances.translation: own rendering from the Latin text at The Latin Library (no pre-1929 English translation of Etymologies Book 18 found)
stances.original: Haec quippe spectacula crudelitatis et inspectio vanitatum non solum hominum vitiis, sed et daemonum iussis instituta sunt. Proinde nihil esse debet Christiano cum Circensi insania, cum inpudicitia theatri, cum amphitheatri crudelitate, cum atrocitate arenae, cum luxuria ludi.
stances.context: Bishop of Seville, died 636. An encyclopedia entry largely drawn from Tertullian's On the Spectacles, written when the great games had mostly died out in the West. He continues: whoever does this "denies God" and returns to what he renounced at the font, "the devil, his pomps and works". Useful as proof that the view stayed standard to the end of the period, not as an independent voice.

stances.summary: The circus drives out serious thought and breeds quarrels, and I do not approve of it. But most people need relief from their cares, so a ruler must sometimes indulge them and pay for the races.
stances.quote: Therefore, as we too must sometimes share the folly of our people, we will freely provide for the expenses of the Circus, however little our judgment approves of this institution.
stances.translation: Thomas Hodgkin, The Letters of Cassiodorus, London: Henry Frowde, 1886 (Hodgkin notes he translated this letter in full)
stances.original: quapropter largiamur expensas, non semper ex iudicio demus. expedit interdum desipere, ut populi possimus desiderata gaudia continere.
stances.location: Book 3, letter 51 (King Theodoric to Faustus, on the charioteer Thomas)
stances.context: Written about 507-511 by Cassiodorus, a Catholic Roman official, in the name of the Ostrogothic king Theodoric (a Homoian, "Arian", Christian); it grants a monthly salary to a star charioteer. So it is the court's official voice, crafted by Cassiodorus. It is the one text found that both condemns the races and defends paying for them, on the ground that the crowd needs relief from its cares. Hodgkin's sentence just before: "We are compelled to support this institution by the necessity of humouring the majority of the people, who are passionately fond of it; for it is always the few who are led by reason, while the many crave excitement and oblivion of their cares." The Latin ends "expedit interdum desipere, ut populi possimus desiderata gaudia continere" (it is sometimes expedient to play the fool, so that we can hold in check the joys the people long for). In Variae 5.42 (523) he laments the beast-fights, but Hodgkin condenses that letter, so do not quote it as his exact words. Cassiodorus later founded the monastery of Vivarium; no later change of view on the games is recorded. Not in the candidate pool.

stances.summary: Games are a good part of life, even on a church feast day. After the night vigil at a saint's shrine we played ball and dice until Mass. I also wrote verses celebrating a friend's win in the circus races.
stances.quote: one shouted for the ball, the other for the board-game, both of which were to be had. I was the leader of the ball-players; you know that book and ball are my twin companions.
stances.translation: O.M. Dalton, The Letters of Sidonius, Oxford, 1915
stances.context: A Gallic aristocrat, later bishop of Clermont (about 470). Dalton dates this letter to 461-467, before he became bishop. The games were played between the dawn Vigils at the tomb of St Justus in Lyons and the Mass at Tierce; a friend rattled dice, which Clement had forbidden. The poem is closer to the claim. In Carmen 23 (to Consentius, about 462-466) Sidonius praises his friend as a winning charioteer in the emperor's New Year circus games and as a connoisseur of pantomime, the very art the Fathers condemned. Lines 304-306 read "nam circensibus ipse quanta ludis / victor gesseris intonante Roma, / laetam par fuit exarare Musam", own rendering: "For the great things you achieved yourself as victor in the circus games, while Rome thundered, deserved a joyful Muse to write them down" (https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/sidoniuscarmina.html, where verse numbers are printed inside the lines). He argues nothing; he simply treats games, races and mime as innocent. The only named early Christian writer found on this side. Not in the candidate pool.

splits_fathers: Almost entirely one-sided. Every early Christian writer found who addresses the public shows says they are not harmless: 22 named voices from Irenaeus, Tatian and Athenagoras (about 170-180) to Isidore (about 630). No early Christian writer was found who argues in his own voice that the shows are innocent. That view survives only as reported by its opponents: Tertullian (On the Spectacles 1-3) and the treatise On the Public Shows (probably Novatian, chapters 1-2) quote fellow believers who called the shows innocent relaxation and cited Elijah's chariot and David's dancing; Clement (Paedagogus 3.11) answers people who call them "a pastime for recreation"; Chrysostom (Homily 37 on Matthew, 9) answers "some, who are nothing hurt by their pastime"; his own congregation left church for the races on Good Friday 399; and Irenaeus (1.6.3) says Valentinian Gnostics attended the gladiators. The nearest named voices on the other side are two late Western laymen: Sidonius Apollinaris (agree in practice: ball and dice on a feast day, a poem praising a friend's circus victory and his taste in pantomime, 460s) and Cassiodorus (mixed: calls the circus folly but funds it because the many need relief from their cares, about 510). Church law shows the same tolerance creeping in: the Council in Trullo (692) bans actors, beast-hunts and theatrical dances for everyone (canon 51), but bans the horse-races only for clergy and monks (canon 24) and during Easter week (canon 66). By kind: the killing-shows (gladiators, beast-fights) are condemned by every Christian who mentions them (Athenagoras: watching a killing is much the same as killing). Plays and mime are condemned almost as universally, for sexual content and the myths of the gods. Races are condemned for frenzy, faction fights, wasted time and pagan origins, yet were tolerated in practice in Christian Constantinople. Sport and play you do yourself are approved: Clement allows wrestling and ball games, Sidonius plays ball, and Cassian records the story of St John resting with a partridge to show the mind needs recreation (Conference 24.21). The Fathers opposed the shows, not fun.
splits_people_today: Most people today, Christian or not, would agree that sport, films, concerts and games are mostly harmless fun, usually adding "depending on what you watch". So the claim as worded is lopsided today toward "agree", while the Fathers are lopsided toward "disagree". It would separate a modern player from the Fathers as a group but would not tell one Father from another. Real minorities disagree in part. Some churches (holiness and Pentecostal churches, many Methodists into the mid-twentieth century, Amish and conservative Mennonites) forbade theatre, cinema or dancing, though most have relaxed these rules. Conservative religious parents object to sexual content. Critics of combat sports and of animal suffering in horse racing, bullfighting or rodeo object to specific shows. Others worry about gambling on sport and about screen and phone habits. Two narrower versions would split modern people far better. First, "What you watch for fun shapes who you become" (Cyprian, Chrysostom, Augustine's Alypius and Novatian all say yes). Second, "Watching violence or sex on screen does no real harm if you know it is not real" (Chrysostom's "tell me not, that what is done is acting" says no).

misattributions.line: What business has a Christian in such places as these? A Christian, who has not the liberty so much as to think of an evil thing.
misattributions.truth: A loose older paraphrase circulating online (for example on gracegems.org) of On the Public Shows 6, a treatise transmitted among Cyprian's works but probably by Novatian. The ANF text reads: "What does a faithful Christian do among these things, since he may not even think upon wickedness?"

misattributions.line: The circus and theater may not improperly be called the chair of pestilence. Away, then, with these lewd, ungodly diversions, which are but impertinence at the best.
misattributions.truth: The first sentence fairly paraphrases Paedagogus 3.11 ("the racecourse and the theatre the seat of plagues"). The second sentence is not in the ANF text; the nearest line is "Let spectacles, therefore, and plays that are full of scurrility and of abundant gossip, be forbidden." Quote the ANF, not the paraphrase.

misattributions.line: cages of immorality and public schools of debauchery
misattributions.truth: A free paraphrase of a real passage, Harmony of the Gospels 1.33, where the NPNF text says the theatres are failing "and with them, too, the dens of vice and the public profession of iniquity". Use the NPNF wording.

misattributions.line: What need have I to speak of the lewdness of the spectacles and be particular in description? For what's there to be met with, but lewd laughing
misattributions.truth: Circulates online (gracegems.org) with no citation. Not found in the Chrysostom homilies checked (Homilies 6 and 37 on Matthew; Against the Games and Theatres). Source unverified; do not use.

misattributions.line: God forbid that Christians should dishonor themselves by such wickedness as this!
misattributions.truth: A paraphrase of To Autolycus 3.15, "But far be it from Christians to conceive any such deeds". In context it follows the charges of cannibalism and adultery as well as the shows, so it is not specifically about entertainment.

misattributions.line: It is not God who gives us to play, but the devil. / Christ never laughed.
misattributions.truth: Genuine (Homily 6 on Matthew, 8: "For it is not God that grants to play, but the devil"; and Christ is seen weeping but "nowhere laugh, nay, nor smile but a little"). But these lines are usually quoted without their context. They answer a man who wants "to laugh and to play all my days", and Chrysostom adds at once that he speaks "not to suppress all laughter". Do not present them as a ban on all play.

misattributions.line: The monk Telemachus ended the gladiatorial games.
misattributions.truth: Theodoret (Ecclesiastical History 5.26, about 450) says the emperor Honorius ended the gladiator shows after Telemachus was stoned about 404. Historians generally treat this as a simplification: the shows seem to have faded over the following decades, and cost and changing taste mattered as much as any single act. Present it as Theodoret's account.

misattributions.line: On the Public Shows (De spectaculis) by Cyprian
misattributions.truth: Printed among Cyprian's works (ANF vol. 5) but generally ascribed to Novatian. Keep Cyprian's own view to To Donatus 7-8 and Epistle 60.
The attribution is disputed. Many scholars now treat the work as an anonymous church order that grew over time, so label the rules on actors and charioteers "attributed to Hippolytus".

notes: 1. The claim as worded is a weak quiz item among the Fathers, because nearly all of them sit on one side. Its value is to separate modern players from the Fathers as a whole. To tell Fathers apart, split the topic. (a) Play and rest: Cassian (Conference 24.21, tr. C.S. Gibson, NPNF2 vol. 11, 1894, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/350824.htm: "unless it sometimes relieved and relaxed the rigour of its purpose by some recreation, the spirit would lose its spring owing to the unbroken strain"), Clement (ball and wrestling), Salvian ("let us laugh... innocently") and Sidonius are for play; Chrysostom's Homily 6 on Matthew leans hard the other way ("it is not God that grants to play"). (b) Public policy: Cassiodorus funds the races as relief for the crowd; Chrysostom wishes the stage pulled down; Ambrose calls lavish sponsorship foolish. (c) What watching does to you: nearly unanimous, but it splits modern people well. 2. Church law, checked (Henry Percival, NPNF2 vol. 14, 1900, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3814.htm). Council in Trullo, canon 24: "No one who is on the priestly catalogue nor any monk is allowed to take part in horse-races or to assist at theatrical representations." Canon 51: "This holy and ecumenical synod altogether forbids those who are called players, and their spectacles, as well as the exhibition of hunts, and the theatrical dances." Canon 66, for Easter week: "Therefore, on the aforesaid days there must not be any horse races or any public spectacle." The Apostolic Constitutions 2.62 (Syria, about 380, anonymous compiler; James Donaldson, ANF vol. 7, 1886, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/07152.htm) says: "Avoid also indecent spectacles: I mean the theatres and the pomps of the heathens". The Councils of Elvira (canon 62) and Arles (314, canons 4-5) also restricted charioteers and actors; not checked in this pass. 3. Alypius (Confessions 6.8) is the best story for a reveal. He detested the gladiators and said "Thus shall I be absent while present", then opened his eyes at a roar from the crowd and was hooked. Augustine had already cured him of his passion for the circus by a chance jibe in class (6.7). 4. The Fathers' critique overlapped with pagan moralists: Cicero on wasteful games (followed by Ambrose), and Seneca, Letter 7, cited in Sanford's notes to Salvian. So the item is not purely "Christian vs world". 5. The anti-show line is often tied to the baptismal promise to renounce "the devil and his pomps" (Tertullian, Salvian, Isidore). That is a theological reason, not just a moral one. 6. Candidate-pool figures with nothing found in this pass (not searched exhaustively): Ignatius, Justin, Perpetua, Hilary, Athanasius, Antony, Ephrem, Macrina, Syncletica, Moses the Black, Arsenius, Poemen, Evagrius, Pelagius, Martin, Paulinus, Benedict, Boethius, Gregory the Great, John Climacus, Isaac the Syrian. Gregory of Nyssa uses spectators at a horse race as a positive picture in the prologue of the Life of Moses, but the only English is modern and it is a metaphor, not a view about the shows. Jacob of Serugh (died 521) wrote Syriac homilies against the theatre, which reportedly quote theatre-goers' excuses, but the only English (C. Moss, Le Museon 1935) is still under copyright and was not read. 7. Telemachus left no words, so he cannot be a result on this item except through Theodoret's account. 8.
